query: For a damaged high-value component made from a material whose physical and microstructural characteristics make traditional fusion-welding repair ineffective because of hot-cracking risk, what intervention could enable continued service without replacing the entire part under aggressive operating conditions? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to traditional fusion-welding repair, the relevant operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Locally applying friction stir processing (FSP) as a solid‐state repair treatment can locally re‐engineer the microstructure of a damaged nickel-based superalloy component—such as one made of Hastelloy‑X or Inconel 713C—to eliminate the critical liquid film and coarse grain conditions that induce hot cracking during fusion welding, thereby enabling the part to continue service under aggressive high‐temperature operating conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐value component fabricated from a nickel‐based superalloy that displays problematic hot‐cracking when fusion welding is attempted. The material possesses a wide solidification interval and heterogeneous grain boundary segregation, making it highly susceptible to liquid film formation and subsequent crack initiation during traditional repair.
generation.intervention: Implement localized friction stir processing (FSP) on the damaged region as a repair technique. Follow the FSP treatment with a tailored post-process heat treatment to further optimize grain boundary characteristics.
generation.conditions: The intervention is performed at ambient temperature using a tool that imparts severe plastic deformation and high strain rate locally in the damaged zone. Subsequently, the repaired component is subjected to high-temperature cyclic loading (e.g., operating at temperatures above 700 °C) to simulate aggressive service conditions typical of aerospace or turbine applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The FSP treatment causes dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement in the repaired zone, significantly reducing the prevalence of low-melting-point liquid films along grain boundaries and homogenizing micro-segregation.
generation.mechanism: FSP, by introducing controlled severe plastic deformation, disrupts the formations that foster hot cracking by eliminating residual liquid films and refining the grain structure. This modification improves ductility and high-temperature resistance, thereby impeding the crack initiation and propagation that are commonly observed in traditional fusion-weld repairs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with fusion-weld repaired regions, the FSP-treated repair area is predicted to exhibit a much lower incidence of hot cracking, improved tensile strength, and enhanced fatigue/creep resistance under high-temperature cyclic stress.
generation.baseline: Traditional fusion-weld repairs typically yield coarse, inhomogeneous microstructures with persistent liquid films at the grain boundaries that rapidly initiate hot cracks, leading to premature failure under aggressive thermal and mechanical loading.
generation.boundary: This FSP-based repair method is expected to be effective in nickel-based superalloys with a significant melting interval and a propensity for grain boundary segregation. Its effectiveness in materials with drastically different thermal properties or under extreme mechanical load conditions outside of the tested temperature range remains to be established.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends findings from friction stir processing studies on hot cracking mitigation in high-strength aluminum alloys (PMC12050289::web::002 and PMC12050289::web::017) and insights on hot cracking in Inconel 713C (PMC8778835::web::002) to the realm of nickel-based superalloy repair. Uncertainty arises due to differences in thermophysical properties between aluminum and nickel alloys and the scaling of FSP parameters, which must be validated for these high-temperature materials.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate test specimens from a nickel-based superalloy (e.g., Inconel 713C) with artificially induced damage representative of in-service cracking. Divide the specimens into two groups: one group receives a traditional fusion-weld repair, while the other group is treated with localized FSP followed by an appropriate heat treatment. Subject both sets to accelerated high-temperature cyclic loading and thermal shock tests that mimic aggressive operating conditions.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of crack incidence and propagation (via microscopy and non-destructive evaluation)
Grain size and grain boundary morphology (via SEM/EBSD)
High-temperature tensile strength and fatigue/creep performance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FSP-repaired specimens do not show a statistically significant improvement (for instance, at least a 20% reduction in crack incidence or superior mechanical performance under the testing conditions) compared to the fusion-weld repaired specimens, then the hypothesis that FSP can mitigate hot cracking and enable continued service will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study establishes friction stir processing (FSP) as a transformative pre-weld treatment for overcoming the persistent challenge of hot cracking in AA6061-T6 fusion welds. By refining the grain structure of the base material, FSP promoted epitaxial growth of fine grains in the fusion zone, reduced dendrite arm spacing, and eliminated macro-solidification cracks. The resultant welds achieved 95% of the tensile strength of the base material after T6 aging, outperforming conventional fusion welding with filler metals and solid-state friction stir welding. This approach unlocks new opportunities for deploying AA6061 in critical applications requiring high-strength, crack-resistant joints, advancing sustainable lightweight manufacturing.

Nickel-based casting alloys are widely used; e.g., in the aviation industry as materials for engine elements such as high- and low-pressure turbine blades, control segments, etc. [,,]. Such components are manufactured by precision casting, which enables castings of a high dimensional accuracy and with the correct shape to be obtained without the need for further mechanical treatment. Analysis of the literature data indicated a considerable proportion of castings are disqualified for use due to identified casting defects in the form of pores, blowholes, shrinkage porosities, or cracks [,]. In the industry, these types of defects are commonly repaired by welding techniques. Analysis of the present knowledge on weldability of nickel-based casting alloys indicated that the main limitation of the repair and remanufacturing of such precision castings is the hot-cracking effect. Hot cracks most often run along the weld/pad weld axis, or as intercrystalline cracks [].
